court: The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section)

holdings.text: Declares the application admissible in respect of the complaint concerning the absence of an interpreter in police custody, and the remainder inadmissible

anchor.surface_text:
FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT, UNANIMOUSLY,

1.  Declares the application admissible in respect of the complaint concerning the absence of an interpreter in police custody, and the remainder inadmissible;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found the complaint about absence of interpreter admissible and dismissed other complaints as inadmissible after examining procedural and substantive grounds.

holdings.text: Holds that there has been a violation of Article 6 § 3 (e) of the Convention taken together with Article 6 § 1

anchor.surface_text: 2.  Holds that there has been a violation of Article 6 § 3 (e) of the Convention taken together with Article 6 § 1;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court held that the failure to provide an interpreter during police custody violated the applicant's right to a fair trial under Article 6 §§1 and 3(e), as the absence impaired her ability to understand charges and make informed decisions.

holdings.text: Holds that the respondent State is to pay the applicant, within three months from the date on which the judgment becomes final in accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, the following amounts: EUR 1,500 in respect of non-pecuniary damage and EUR 1,300 in respect of costs and expenses, plus interest
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court awarded just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage and costs, reasoning that these amounts were reasonable and appropriate given the violation found.

holdings.text: Dismisses the remainder of the applicant’s claim for just satisfaction

anchor.surface_text: 4.  Dismisses the remainder of the applicant’s claim for just satisfaction.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court rejected other claims for just satisfaction beyond those awarded for non-pecuniary damage and costs.

anchor.surface_text: ...following an acquittal or the quashing of a conviction, the applicant cannot be considered a “victim” of a violation of the rights guaranteed by Article 6 of the Convention (see Bouglamé v. Belgium (dec.), no. 16147/08, 2 March 2010, and the numerous references therein).

precedents.cited_proposition: An applicant cannot be considered a victim of a violation of Article 6 rights following an acquittal or quashing of conviction.

anchor.surface_text: ...This means that an accused who cannot understand or speak the language used in court has the right to the free assistance of an interpreter for the translation or interpretation of all those documents or statements in the proceedings instituted against him which it is necessary for him to understand or to have rendered into the court’s language in order to have the benefit of a fair trial (see Luedicke, Belkacem and Koç v. Germany, 28 November 1978, § 48, Series A no. 29).

precedents.case_name: Luedicke, Belkacem and Koç v. Germany
precedents.cited_proposition: Right to free assistance of an interpreter for translation or interpretation of documents or statements necessary for a fair trial.

anchor.surface_text: ...Furthermore, the interpretation assistance provided should be such as to enable the accused to have knowledge of the case against him and to defend himself, notably by being able to put before the court his version of the events (see Güngör v. Germany (dec.), no. 31540/96, 17 May 2001).

precedents.cited_proposition: Interpretation assistance should enable the accused to know the case and defend himself, including presenting his version of events.

anchor.surface_text: ...that of an interpreter should be provided from the investigation stage, unless it is demonstrated that there are compelling reasons to restrict this right (see, to that effect, Diallo v. Sweden (dec.), no. 13205/07, § 25, 5 January 2010).

precedents.cited_proposition: Right to interpreter assistance from investigation stage unless compelling reasons to restrict it.

anchor.surface_text: ...the Court has already had occasion to emphasise the importance of the investigation stage for the preparation of the criminal proceedings, as the evidence obtained at this stage may be decisive for the subsequent proceedings (see, to that effect, Salduz v. Turkey [GC], no. 36391/02, § 63, ECHR 2008).

precedents.cited_proposition: Investigation stage is crucial as evidence obtained may be decisive for subsequent proceedings.

precedents.citation: Cuscani v. the United Kingdom, no. 32771/96, § 38, 24 September 2002

anchor.surface_text: ...the judge apparently failed to verify the skills of that interpreter, who was simply a member of the applicant’s family waiting in the corridor (see, mutatis mutandis, Cuscani v. the United Kingdom, no. 32771/96, § 38, 24 September 2002, and paragraph 19 above).

precedents.cited_proposition: Court must verify interpreter's skills; failure to do so is problematic.

anchor.surface_text: ...a re-trial or the reopening of the proceedings, at the request of the person concerned, represents in principle an appropriate means of redress for the violation in question (see Gençel v. Turkey, no. 53431/99, § 27, 23 October 2003).

precedents.cited_proposition: Re-trial or reopening proceedings is appropriate redress for violation of rights.

outcome.relief_summary: Violation of Article 6 § 3 (e) taken with Article 6 § 1 found; awarded EUR 1,500 non-pecuniary damage and EUR 1,300 costs and expenses; remainder of just satisfaction claim dismissed.
directions: Respondent State to pay specified amounts within three months from judgment finality date.
Simple interest payable on amounts from expiry of three months until settlement at ECB marginal lending rate plus three percentage points.
